prompt: Each card is one thing a consumer says or does about a brand. Is it affect, behavior, or cognition?

cards.text: "I just love the smell of this shampoo."
cards.explanation: Affect: a feeling toward the product.

cards.text: "Flying with that airline makes me nervous."
cards.explanation: Affect: an emotion toward the brand.

cards.text: "I feel proud every time I ride my new bike."
cards.explanation: Affect: a feeling the object brings up.

cards.text: Ana tells her sister to try the café on the corner.
cards.explanation: Behavior: recommending is an action toward the brand.

cards.text: Omar walks past the energy drink he had a bad experience with.
cards.explanation: Behavior: avoiding a brand is an action.

cards.text: "I'm going to buy that laptop when it goes on sale."
cards.explanation: Behavior: an intention to buy counts as behavior.

cards.text: "I believe this phone's battery lasts two full days."
cards.explanation: Cognition: a belief about the product.

cards.text: "That store brand costs less than the national brand."
cards.explanation: Cognition: a thought about the product's price.

cards.text: "I think this yogurt is made locally."
cards.explanation: Cognition: a belief about where the product comes from.

prompt: Match each function of attitudes with the consumer whose attitude serves it.

pairs.match: Lena likes her bank because it charges no monthly fees.
pairs.explanation: Utilitarian: the attitude rests on gaining a benefit and avoiding a cost.

pairs.match: Malik wears only second-hand clothes to show that he cares about the planet.
pairs.explanation: Value-expressive: the attitude communicates his values and self-image.

pairs.match: Before a first date, Jo buys a strong mouthwash so she won't feel embarrassed.
pairs.explanation: Ego-defensive: the attitude protects her self-esteem from an uncomfortable threat.

pairs.match: In a country he has never visited, Chen picks the one supermarket chain he recognizes, because he knows what to expect inside.
pairs.explanation: Knowledge: the attitude organizes information and makes an unfamiliar situation easier to understand.

prompt: Each case describes how an attitude formed. Which hierarchy is it?

cases.text: Before buying a refrigerator, Sara compares energy ratings and reviews for weeks, comes to prefer one model, and then buys it.
cases.explanation: Standard learning: think, feel, then act.

cases.text: Tom grabs a pack of batteries at the checkout after a glance at the price. Only after using them does he decide he likes the brand.
cases.explanation: Low involvement: think briefly, act, then develop a feeling.

cases.text: Mia hears a song she loves, buys concert tickets on the spot, and later tells friends the band's lyrics are clever.
Raj reads every policy detail for three insurers, decides which one he trusts, and then signs up.
cases.explanation: Standard learning: beliefs come first, then a feeling, then the purchase.

cases.text: Elena tries on a jacket, loves how it feels, buys it, and only at home lists its good points to herself.
cases.explanation: Experiential: the feeling leads, the action follows, and the explanation comes last.

cases.text: Leo picks the dish soap on the end of the aisle without much thought. After a month of using it, he finds he prefers it.
cases.explanation: Low involvement: a brief thought, a purchase, then a feeling.

prompt: Each card describes the source of a message. Does its impact come from expertise, trustworthiness, or attractiveness?

cards.text: A dentist explains how a toothpaste protects enamel.
cards.explanation: Expertise: the source seems knowledgeable.

cards.text: A race-car mechanic recommends a brand of motor oil.
cards.explanation: Expertise: the source knows the subject.

cards.text: A reviewer admits the headphones feel tight but still recommends them.
cards.explanation: Trustworthiness: naming a downside makes the source seem honest.

cards.text: A blogger says she paid for the stroller herself and was not sponsored.
cards.explanation: Trustworthiness: the source seems honest and dependable.

cards.text: A campus ad shows a student who looks and talks like the students watching it.
cards.explanation: Attractiveness: similarity between the source and the audience.

cards.text: An actor viewers have seen in many commercials appears in a new one.
cards.explanation: Attractiveness: familiarity with the source.

cards.text: A cheerful, friendly TV host presents a cooking brand.
cards.explanation: Attractiveness: likability of the source.

prompt: Each case shows a consumer taking advice from an AI system. Is it algorithm aversion, algorithm appreciation, or an AI that seems expert but not trustworthy?

cases.text: After a weather app wrongly predicts sun once, Priya stops checking it. Her neighbor's forecasts are wrong just as often, but she still asks him.
cases.explanation: Algorithm aversion: after one mistake, she loses confidence in the algorithm faster than in the person.

cases.text: Asked to guess the calories in a meal, Ben changes his answer more when the suggested number is labelled as coming from an algorithm than when it is labelled as coming from another diner.
cases.explanation: Algorithm appreciation: for a numerical estimate, he follows advice more when it comes from an algorithm.

cases.text: A travel assistant knows every flight and fare, but Kim cannot tell whether it is paid to push one airline, so she double-checks every suggestion.
cases.explanation: The AI seems expert but not trustworthy, because Kim does not know whose interests it serves.

cases.text: Carlos's navigation app sends him into one traffic jam, and he switches it off for good, though he keeps following a friend who gave him a bad route last week.
cases.explanation: Algorithm aversion: the same mistake costs the algorithm more trust than the person.

cases.text: Estimating how much paint a room needs, Nadia takes the algorithm's number over the store clerk's.
cases.explanation: Algorithm appreciation: in a numerical estimate, she follows the algorithm's advice.

cases.text: A shopping agent gives detailed, accurate product comparisons, but Aisha does not know whether the store that runs it ranks its own products first.
cases.explanation: Expert but not trustworthy: credibility needs trustworthiness, and she does not know whose interests the agent serves.

prompt: Each card is a line from a message. Is it a positive frame or a negative frame?

cards.text: "Get a brighter smile in two weeks."
cards.explanation: Positive frame: it emphasizes a desirable result.

cards.text: "Don't lose your photos when your phone breaks."
cards.explanation: Negative frame: it emphasizes a loss that may follow inaction.

cards.text: "Earn double points on every purchase this month."
cards.explanation: Positive frame: it emphasizes a gain.

cards.text: "Without sunscreen, one afternoon can damage your skin for years."
cards.explanation: Negative frame: it emphasizes a risk.

cards.text: "95% fat-free."
cards.explanation: Positive frame: it presents the fact as a benefit.

cards.text: "Every day without insulation, heat leaks out of your home."
cards.explanation: Negative frame: it emphasizes the problem that follows inaction.

cards.text: "Wake up with more energy every morning."
cards.explanation: Positive frame: it emphasizes a benefit.

cards.text: "Stop paying late fees you could have avoided."
cards.explanation: Negative frame: it emphasizes a cost.

question_text: A brand team wants to know how a shopping assistant's AI model feels about its products. They ask the model once to rate "This brand is trustworthy" on a 1–7 scale, and it answers 6. Which conclusion fits the slide?
hint: Think about how a model answers the same question more than once, and what an attitude in a model is.
correct_answer_citation: Week 06 · Measuring the Attitudes of AI Models

options.option_text: The model's attitude toward the brand is 6, so the team can report it
options.option_explanation: A model does not give one fixed answer. A single answer can mislead.

options.option_text: The model feels warmly toward the brand
options.option_explanation: An attitude in a model is a pattern in its answers. It is not a feeling that the model experiences.

options.option_text: The team should ask the same question many times, or read the probability the model assigns to each point, before drawing a conclusion
options.option_explanation: Correct. Reliable measurement asks the question many times, or reads the probability the model assigns to each point on the scale.

options.option_text: Any other developer's model would give the same rating, so one model is enough
options.option_explanation: Measured reliably, models from different developers held different attitudes on the same consumer attitude scale.
